content: The guidelines on long-acting injectable cabotegravir (CAB-LA) for HIV prevention provide detailed insights into its potential impact on reducing HIV transmission when used as part of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) strategies. CAB-LA has demonstrated superior efficacy compared to daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) in the HPTN 083 and 084 trials and was approved for HIV prevention in the United States in December 2021. A comparative modeling analysis was conducted to evaluate the potential population-level impact of expanding PrEP coverage by offering CAB-LA in different settings. The analysis focused on two key populations: men who have sex with men (MSM) in Atlanta, USA, and Montreal, Canada—cities with concentrated HIV epidemics dominated by MSM transmission—and cisgender men and women in South Africa, a country with a generalized HIV epidemic. Methods: Four independent HIV transmission models, stratified by age and risk, were calibrated to local data from Atlanta (HPTN model), Montreal (McGill model), and South Africa (Synthesis and Thembisa models). The models simulated the expansion of PrEP coverage over 5 and 10 years by recruiting additional PrEP users based on current PrEP eligibility criteria and switching varying proportions of TDF/FTC users to CAB-LA starting in 2022. The analysis evaluated population effectiveness, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness of PrEP expansion over 20 years compared to baseline scenarios with only TDF/FTC use. Findings for MSM in Atlanta and Montreal: 1. Baseline PrEP Coverage: In the base-case scenarios, overall PrEP coverage was projected to increase modestly from 30% to 32% in Atlanta and from 6% to 10% in Montreal between 2022 and 2042. 2. Impact of CAB-LA Expansion: Increasing PrEP coverage by 8–10 percentage points to 40% of the MSM population in Atlanta by 2027 could avert 35–39% of new HIV infections over 20 years. In Montreal, a larger increase in PrEP coverage (~20 percentage points to 30%) would be required to avert a comparable fraction of infections due to high population-level viral suppression. 3. Cost-Effectiveness: The cost to avert one disability-adjusted life year (DALY) was estimated at approximately $200,000 in Atlanta and significantly higher in Montreal, reaching millions of US dollars. Achieving 50% PrEP coverage by 2027 could avert nearly 60% of new HIV infections over 20 years in both settings. 4. Efficiency and Feasibility: Offering CAB-LA to MSM in the USA and Canada could substantially impact the HIV epidemic if it leads to increased overall PrEP coverage. However, while PrEP expansion could be highly efficient and potentially cost-effective in high-incidence settings like Atlanta, it is unlikely to be cost-effective in low-incidence settings like Montreal. Findings for South Africa: 1. Baseline PrEP Coverage: Median overall PrEP coverage in South Africa is currently at or below 1% and is not expected to increase significantly by 2042 under base-case scenarios. 2. Impact of CAB-LA Expansion: Increasing PrEP coverage to 13% of the adult population by 2027, primarily targeting high-risk groups, could avert approximately 20% of new HIV infections over 20 years (Thembisa model). Achieving 5% CAB-LA coverage among high-risk groups with targeted use during periods of substantial HIV risk could avert nearly 50% of new infections over 20 years (Synthesis model). 3. Comparison with TDF/FTC: Expanding PrEP coverage with oral TDF/FTC instead of CAB-LA is expected to reduce the impact by up to 20% (Thembisa model) and 40% (Synthesis model) due to lower efficacy and adherence. 4. Efficiency of CAB-LA: Approximately 16–25 additional person-years (PYs) on CAB-LA are needed to prevent one infection in South Africa with strict risk targeting (Synthesis model), compared to over 100 PYs if CAB-LA is broadly available but predominantly used by high-risk individuals (Thembisa model). 5. Cost-Effectiveness: Offering CAB-LA in South Africa could significantly impact the HIV epidemic if adequately used by individuals at high risk of acquiring HIV. PrEP expansion could be highly efficient and cost-effective if adopted primarily during periods of substantial risk. Conclusion: The analysis highlights the potential of CAB-LA to substantially reduce HIV transmission when integrated into PrEP programs, particularly in high-incidence settings. However, the cost-effectiveness of CAB-LA varies significantly depending on the epidemiological context, with greater efficiency observed in settings with high HIV incidence and targeted use among high-risk populations. Expanding PrEP coverage with CAB-LA could be a transformative strategy for HIV prevention, provided it is implemented with careful consideration of local epidemiological and economic factors.
